Title: [from] Suki's Kimono
Author: by Chieri Uegaki
Content: On the `text(first)` day of school, Suki wanted to wear her kimono¹. Her sisters did not approve.
“You can't wear that,” said Mari. “People will think you're weird.”
“You can't wear that,” said Yumi. “Everyone will laugh, and no one will play with you.”
But Suki shook her head. She didn't care for new. She didn't care for cool. She wanted to wear her favorite thing. And her favorite thing was her kimono.

Suki's obāchan² had given her the kimono. The `text(first)` time Suki wore it, her obāchan took her to a street festival where they slurped bowls of slippery, cold sōmen noodles³ and shared a cone of crunchy, shaved ice topped with a sweet red bean sauce.

Under strings of paper lanterns, Suki joined her obāchan in a circle dance. She followed her and copied her movements, trying to be as light and as graceful. She watched the other women and children who danced, especially those who were dressed in cotton kimonos like her.
Later, Suki sat so close to the stage that when the taiko⁴ drummers performed, bom-bom-bom-bom, she felt like she'd swallowed a ball of thunder and her whole insides quaked and quivered.

Before they left the festival, Suki and her obāchan stopped at a souvenir stand. There were many things to choose from, but her obāchan found the prettiest thing of all-a handkerchief of pale pink linen, decorated with tiny maple leaves and cherry blossoms. When she gave it to Suki, she said, “This will help you remember our `text(day)`.”
Now, it was time for school. Mother checked Suki's obi⁵ `text(one)` last time and took a picture of Mari, Yumi and Suki together by the front steps.
Then, as she watched, the `text(three)` sisters made their way down the block to their school. Mari and Yumi stayed several paces ahead of Suki and pretended they didn't know her.
She turned and waved to her mother before she clip-clopped along in her shiny red geta⁶, feeling very pleased in her fan-patterned blue kimono.

References: kimono - the Japanese name for a loose wraparound robe with wide sleeves
obāchan - a Japanese word for grandmother
sōmen noodles - very thin Japanese noodles
taiko - the name of a Japanese drum
obi - a kimono sash or a wide belt
geta - Japanese wooden clogs or shoes
